units.text: If we learned the universe is simulated, what exactly would we have learned? That matter has a different substrate from the one imagined? That authors exist? That they can intervene? That the world’s purpose is an experiment? These conclusions are often packaged together although the first does not prove all the others.

First, three ideas must be separated. The world can be described computationally. The world can have fundamental dynamics resembling computation. The world can be implemented in another system as a simulation made for particular purposes. Using computers to describe gravity does not prove gravity is produced by an external computer.

Nor is opposition between emergence and simulation mandatory. Emergent effective laws can arise within a simulation. A nonsimulated system could have simple discrete rules. A simulator could implement continuous or probabilistic processes through methods unlike our video games. The two questions differ: how do a level’s regularities arise, and on what substrate is that level realized?

Nick Bostrom’s argument is more precise than the popular formula ‘we probably live in a game’. In a conditional scheme, it links three possibilities: civilizations like ours rarely reach the relevant capability; those reaching it produce very few ancestor simulations; or simulated observers of the relevant type greatly outnumber nonsimulated ones. Moving to a belief about ourselves nevertheless requires assumptions about consciousness, resources, civilizations’ behavior and the observer class from which we consider ourselves a sample (Bostrom, 2003) .

It does not follow that the three alternatives have equal probabilities. A disjunction containing three statements does not allocate one third of reality to each. Nor does technical ability to simulate a process prove that the simulated process has conscious experience. These difficulties are part of evaluating the argument, not details to leave until after the conclusion.

We can construct an arithmetic example without claiming it describes the cosmos. If there are a thousand nonsimulated observers and a million simulated observers of a comparable type, a uniform sample from their union will almost always be simulated. But why should our situation be equivalent to that uniform sample? How do we define ‘comparable’? Do we count people, moments of experience, identical copies or worlds? The arithmetic is simple; justifying the sampling scheme is not.

Another vocabulary error appears. A simulation need not be ‘unreal’ to its inhabitants. Chalmers argues that a Matrix-type hypothesis can change the world’s metaphysics without making all ordinary judgments about its objects and relations false. If an object has stability and causal roles in our world, discovering a computational substrate may change what we believe it fundamentally is, not the fact that we can bump into it (Chalmers, 2003/2005) .

Nevertheless, simulating an environment for an external brain must be distinguished from minds themselves implemented within a simulation. The first presupposes a mind on another substrate; the second presupposes that simulated organization can sustain experience. Arguments about consciousness cannot be resolved simply by counting characters generated in a program.

Intervention is not mandatory either. A program can be left to evolve, receive inputs or be modified. Its creator may have complete control, limited control or no longer exist. Deducing ‘constantly supervised by an omnipotent intelligence’ from ‘implemented’ imports a theology without argument.

What do we gain intellectually from the hypothesis? It forces us to distinguish internal law from implementation mechanism, prediction from ontology and experience from substrate. What do we risk? Turning every surprise into a message and every absence of evidence into evidence of simulation’s perfection. In the latter case, the hypothesis becomes immune to experience.

The serious question is therefore not ‘can it be imagined?’ It can. The question is which precise version we choose, what it adds to an internal physical description and which observations should differ. Without this step, we have a possible metaphysics. With it, some variants can become research programs.
